questions.question: Photolysis of water takes place in the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis. Which of the following are produced directly by the photolysis of water? A glucose and oxygen, B protons, electrons and oxygen, C protons, electrons and carbon dioxide, D ATP and reduced NADP.
questions.answer: B: protons, electrons and oxygen
steps: Photolysis uses light energy to split water: 2H2O -> 4H+ + 4e- + O2.
The electrons replace those lost from chlorophyll in photosystem II, the protons contribute to the proton gradient and to the reduction of NADP, and oxygen is released as a waste product.

A is wrong because glucose is made from the products of the Calvin cycle; C is wrong because carbon dioxide is a reactant in the Calvin cycle, not a product of photolysis; D is wrong because ATP and reduced NADP are made later, by the electron transport chain, not by photolysis itself.

questions.question: Which statement about the light-independent reactions of photosynthesis is correct? A ATP is used to regenerate ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP) from triose phosphate, B reduced NADP is used to oxidise glycerate 3-phosphate (GP) to triose phosphate, C rubisco catalyses the conversion of GP to triose phosphate, D one molecule of carbon dioxide combines with one molecule of RuBP to form one molecule of GP.
questions.answer: A: ATP is used to regenerate RuBP from triose phosphate
steps: Regenerating RuBP from triose phosphate needs ATP from the light-dependent reactions, so A is correct.
B is wrong because reduced NADP reduces GP to triose phosphate; it is not used to oxidise it.
C is wrong because rubisco catalyses the combination of carbon dioxide with RuBP, not the reduction of GP.
D is wrong because one carbon dioxide and one RuBP give two molecules of GP.

questions.question: A leaf is kept in saturating light and a high concentration of carbon dioxide. The rate of photosynthesis increases when the temperature is raised from 15 degrees C to 25 degrees C, but decreases when the temperature is raised to 45 degrees C. Explain these changes in the rate of photosynthesis.
questions.answer: The rate rises to 25 degrees C because the enzyme-controlled Calvin cycle reactions speed up with more kinetic energy; at 45 degrees C enzymes such as rubisco are denatured.
steps: From 15 to 25 degrees C molecules have more kinetic energy, so more frequent collisions between enzyme and substrate
More enzyme-substrate complexes form per second, so the rate of the enzyme-controlled light-independent reactions (e.g. rubisco) increases
At 45 degrees C hydrogen bonds / bonds holding the tertiary structure break, changing the shape of the active site
Substrate no longer complementary to the active site / enzymes (e.g. rubisco) denatured, so the rate of photosynthesis falls
accept: Light and carbon dioxide are not limiting, so the temperature-sensitive enzyme-controlled stage sets the rate
More collisions with enough energy to react (activation energy) at the higher temperature
Fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form at 45 degrees C
Thylakoid membrane proteins / enzymes of the light-dependent reactions may also be damaged at 45 degrees C

questions.question: Compare and contrast cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
questions.answer: Both make ATP by chemiosmosis from electrons passed along carriers; only non-cyclic uses photosystem II and photolysis and also makes reduced NADP and oxygen.
steps: Similarity: both make ATP by photophosphorylation / chemiosmosis (excited electrons pass along an electron transport chain, protons are pumped, ATP synthase)
Non-cyclic uses photosystems I and II (and photolysis of water), whereas cyclic uses photosystem I only
Non-cyclic also produces reduced NADP and oxygen, whereas cyclic produces ATP only
accept: In non-cyclic the electrons are replaced from water; in cyclic the electrons return to the photosystem / chlorophyll
Non-cyclic is a one-way flow of electrons ending at NADP; in cyclic the electron path is a loop
Both take place in the thylakoid membranes (grana)

questions.question: In a chromatography experiment to separate the pigments in a leaf extract, the solvent front moved 8.5 cm from the origin. The centre of the spot of chlorophyll a was 5.1 cm from the origin. Calculate the Rf value of chlorophyll a.
steps: Rf = distance moved by the pigment / distance moved by the solvent front.
Rf = 5.1 / 8.5 = 0.60 (it has no units because it is a ratio).

questions.question: A suspension of the alga Chlorella was given a constant supply of carbon dioxide and kept in bright light. When the light was switched off, the concentration of glycerate 3-phosphate (GP) in the algae increased and the concentration of ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP) decreased. Explain these changes.
questions.answer: With no light, no ATP or reduced NADP is made, so GP is not reduced and RuBP is not regenerated; rubisco still uses up RuBP, so GP rises and RuBP falls.
steps: No light, so the light-dependent reactions stop / no ATP or reduced NADP is made
GP cannot be reduced to triose phosphate (needs ATP and reduced NADP), so GP accumulates / its concentration rises
RuBP is not regenerated from triose phosphate (needs ATP)
Rubisco still combines carbon dioxide with the RuBP already present, forming GP
So RuBP is used up / its concentration falls
accept: The concentration of triose phosphate also falls because GP is no longer converted to it
Carbon dioxide is still supplied, so carbon fixation continues until the RuBP has run out
Reduced NADP supplies the hydrogen / electrons for reducing GP and is no longer available

questions.question: A student investigated the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis of the pondweed Elodea. She placed a lamp at different distances from a beaker of water containing a shoot of pondweed and collected the oxygen released in a gas syringe for 15 minutes. She collected 2.10 cm3 of oxygen with the lamp 10 cm from the beaker, 0.60 cm3 with the lamp 20 cm away and 0.15 cm3 with the lamp 40 cm away. Calculate the mean rate of oxygen production when the lamp was 10 cm from the beaker. Give your answer in mm3 min^-1.
questions.answer: 140 mm3 min^-1

questions.question: A student investigated the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis of the pondweed Elodea. She placed a lamp at different distances from a beaker of water containing a shoot of pondweed and collected the oxygen released in a gas syringe for 15 minutes. She collected 2.10 cm3 of oxygen with the lamp 10 cm from the beaker, 0.60 cm3 with the lamp 20 cm away and 0.15 cm3 with the lamp 40 cm away. Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the lamp. Show that the light intensity at 10 cm was 16 times the light intensity at 40 cm.
questions.answer: Intensity at 10 cm / intensity at 40 cm = (40/10)^2 = 16
steps: Intensity is proportional to 1 / distance^2, so I(10) / I(40) = 40^2 / 10^2.

questions.question: A student investigated the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis of the pondweed Elodea. She placed a lamp at different distances from a beaker of water containing a shoot of pondweed and collected the oxygen released in a gas syringe for 15 minutes. She collected 2.10 cm3 of oxygen with the lamp 10 cm from the beaker, 0.60 cm3 with the lamp 20 cm away and 0.15 cm3 with the lamp 40 cm away. The volume of oxygen collected with the lamp at 10 cm was 14 times the volume collected with the lamp at 40 cm (2.10 / 0.15 = 14), not 16 times. Suggest why the rate of photosynthesis did not increase in proportion to the light intensity.
questions.answer: At the highest light intensity another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, became limiting.
steps: At 10 cm light was no longer the (only) limiting factor, so the rate was no longer proportional to light intensity
Another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, was limiting the rate
The light-dependent reactions made ATP and reduced NADP faster than the enzyme-controlled Calvin cycle could use them, so more light had little further effect
accept: The amount of rubisco / other enzymes limited the rate
Carbon dioxide dissolved in the water was used up faster at the higher rate of photosynthesis
The photosystems were saturated with light
Heat from the lamp at 10 cm may have raised the temperature above the optimum for the enzymes

questions.question: A student investigated the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis of the pondweed Elodea. She placed a lamp at different distances from a beaker of water containing a shoot of pondweed and collected the oxygen released in a gas syringe for 15 minutes. She collected 2.10 cm3 of oxygen with the lamp 10 cm from the beaker, 0.60 cm3 with the lamp 20 cm away and 0.15 cm3 with the lamp 40 cm away. The lamp gave out heat as well as light. Describe two changes to the method that would improve the validity of the results.
questions.answer: Place a heat shield (a glass tank of water) between the lamp and the beaker to keep the temperature constant, and add sodium hydrogencarbonate to the water so that carbon dioxide is not limiting.
steps: Place a heat shield (glass tank of water) between the lamp and the beaker / use a cool LED lamp, so the temperature stays constant
Add sodium hydrogencarbonate to the water so the carbon dioxide concentration is constant (not limiting)
accept: Use a thermostatically controlled water bath for the beaker
Allow the pondweed to equilibrate for a few minutes at each distance before collecting gas
Repeat at each distance and calculate a mean
Use the same shoot (same length / leaf area) for every distance

questions.question: Which statement about glycolysis in a liver cell is correct? A It occurs in the mitochondrial matrix and gives a net yield of 2 ATP per molecule of glucose, B It occurs in the cytoplasm and gives a net yield of 2 ATP per molecule of glucose, C It occurs in the cytoplasm and gives a net yield of 4 ATP per molecule of glucose, D It occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane and gives a net yield of about 30 ATP per molecule of glucose.
questions.answer: B: it occurs in the cytoplasm and gives a net yield of 2 ATP
steps: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm; 2 ATP are used to phosphorylate glucose and 4 ATP are made, so the net yield is 2 ATP.
A is wrong because glycolysis does not occur in the mitochondrial matrix.
C quotes the gross yield (4 ATP) without subtracting the 2 ATP used.
D describes oxidative phosphorylation (inner mitochondrial membrane, large ATP yield), not glycolysis.

questions.question: Which of the following gives the products formed in one turn of the Krebs cycle? A 3 reduced NAD, 1 reduced FAD and 1 ATP, B 1 reduced NAD, 3 reduced FAD and 1 ATP, C 3 reduced NAD, 1 reduced FAD and 2 ATP, D 6 reduced NAD, 2 reduced FAD and 2 ATP.
questions.answer: A: 3 reduced NAD, 1 reduced FAD and 1 ATP
steps: One turn of the cycle produces 3 reduced NAD, 1 reduced FAD and 1 ATP (by substrate-level phosphorylation), as well as 2 carbon dioxide.
B swaps the numbers of reduced NAD and reduced FAD.
C gives the wrong number of ATP.
D gives the totals for two turns of the cycle, which is the number needed for one molecule of glucose, not one turn.

questions.question: Describe what happens to pyruvate in the link reaction.
questions.answer: Pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix, is decarboxylated (carbon dioxide released) and dehydrogenated (NAD reduced), and the 2-carbon acetyl group joins coenzyme A to form acetyl CoA.
steps: Decarboxylation: carbon dioxide is removed from pyruvate
Dehydrogenation / oxidation: hydrogen is removed and accepted by NAD, forming reduced NAD
The 2-carbon acetyl group combines with coenzyme A to form acetyl CoA
accept: Takes place in the mitochondrial matrix
Pyruvate is first transported into the mitochondrion from the cytoplasm
Acetyl CoA is carried to (enters) the Krebs cycle
The link reaction occurs twice per glucose molecule

questions.question: The complete oxidation of one mole of glucose releases 2803 kJ. In a liver cell, the aerobic respiration of one mole of glucose produces 32 moles of ATP, and the hydrolysis of one mole of ATP releases 30.5 kJ. Calculate the percentage of the energy released from the glucose that is transferred to ATP. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
steps: Energy transferred to ATP = 32 x 30.5 = 976 kJ.
Percentage = 976 / 2803 x 100 = 34.8%, which is 35% to 2 significant figures.

questions.question: Explain why the conversion of pyruvate to lactate allows a muscle cell to go on making ATP by glycolysis when oxygen is not available.
questions.answer: Reduced NAD is oxidised back to NAD when pyruvate is reduced to lactate, so NAD is available and glycolysis can continue to make ATP.
steps: Without oxygen the electron transport chain cannot reoxidise reduced NAD
Pyruvate accepts hydrogen from reduced NAD and is reduced to lactate (reduced NAD is oxidised to NAD)
NAD is regenerated and is available to oxidise triose phosphate in glycolysis, so glycolysis can continue to make (net 2) ATP
accept: Lactate dehydrogenase catalyses the conversion
Without NAD glycolysis would stop and no ATP would be made
Pyruvate acts as the hydrogen acceptor
The ATP from glycolysis allows muscle contraction to continue for a short time

questions.question: Compare and contrast anaerobic respiration in yeast cells with anaerobic respiration in mammalian muscle cells.
questions.answer: Both use glycolysis and regenerate NAD from reduced NAD; yeast converts pyruvate to ethanal (releasing carbon dioxide) and then ethanol, whereas muscle cells convert pyruvate directly to lactate.
steps: Both begin with glycolysis (glucose to pyruvate, net 2 ATP)
Both oxidise reduced NAD to NAD, so that glycolysis can continue
Difference: yeast decarboxylates pyruvate to ethanal (releasing CO2) and reduces ethanal to ethanol, whereas muscle reduces pyruvate directly to lactate with no CO2 released
accept: Yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide; muscle produces lactate only
Lactate can be converted back to pyruvate when oxygen is available (e.g. in the liver)
Both take place in the cytoplasm
Different enzymes: pyruvate decarboxylase and ethanol dehydrogenase in yeast, lactate dehydrogenase in muscle

questions.question: Cyanide is a poison that prevents the transfer of electrons to oxygen at the end of the electron transport chain in mitochondria. Explain the effects of cyanide on the production of ATP in a muscle cell.
questions.answer: The chain stops, the proton gradient and oxidative phosphorylation stop, NAD and FAD are not regenerated so the link reaction and Krebs cycle stop, and the cell is left with only the small ATP yield of glycolysis.
steps: Electrons cannot be passed to oxygen, so the electron transport chain stops (carriers stay reduced)
No energy is released to pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane / the proton gradient is lost
ATP synthase cannot make ATP: no oxidative phosphorylation (chemiosmosis)
Reduced NAD and reduced FAD are not reoxidised, so NAD and FAD are not regenerated
Link reaction and Krebs cycle stop (they need NAD / FAD), so there is no ATP from substrate-level phosphorylation in the Krebs cycle
The cell relies on glycolysis, which gives only a net 2 ATP per glucose, so ATP production falls greatly
accept: Oxygen is not used / not reduced to water
Lactate builds up as the cell switches to anaerobic respiration
Protons are not pumped out of the matrix, so none flow back through ATP synthase
The muscle cell cannot contract properly (or may die) through lack of ATP

questions.question: A student used a respirometer to measure the rate of oxygen uptake of 2.0 g of germinating pea seeds. The seeds were in a sealed tube that also contained a small container of potassium hydroxide solution, which absorbs carbon dioxide. The tube was connected to a horizontal capillary tube of internal diameter 1.0 mm containing a drop of coloured fluid. The fluid moved 36 mm towards the seeds in 12 minutes at a constant temperature. Explain why the coloured fluid moved towards the seeds.
questions.answer: The seeds used oxygen and the carbon dioxide they produced was absorbed, so the volume of gas in the tube and the pressure fell and the fluid moved towards the seeds.
steps: Seeds take up oxygen in respiration and the carbon dioxide produced is absorbed by the potassium hydroxide
The volume / pressure of gas in the tube decreases, so the fluid moves towards the seeds
accept: The higher outside pressure pushes the fluid along the tube
The net decrease in gas volume equals the volume of oxygen consumed

questions.question: A student used a respirometer to measure the rate of oxygen uptake of 2.0 g of germinating pea seeds. The seeds were in a sealed tube that also contained a small container of potassium hydroxide solution, which absorbs carbon dioxide. The tube was connected to a horizontal capillary tube of internal diameter 1.0 mm containing a drop of coloured fluid. The fluid moved 36 mm towards the seeds in 12 minutes at a constant temperature. Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake of the seeds in mm3 g^-1 min^-1. The volume of a cylinder is pi x r^2 x h. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
steps: Radius of the capillary tube = 0.5 mm, so volume of oxygen taken up = pi x 0.5^2 x 36 = 28.3 mm3.
Rate of uptake = 28.3 / 12 = 2.36 mm3 min^-1.
Rate per gram of seeds = 2.36 / 2.0 = 1.2 mm3 g^-1 min^-1 (2 s.f.).

questions.question: A student used a respirometer to measure the rate of oxygen uptake of 2.0 g of germinating pea seeds. The seeds were in a sealed tube that also contained a small container of potassium hydroxide solution, which absorbs carbon dioxide. The tube was connected to a horizontal capillary tube of internal diameter 1.0 mm containing a drop of coloured fluid. The fluid moved 36 mm towards the seeds in 12 minutes at a constant temperature. The student repeated the experiment using 2.0 g of seeds that had been boiled and then cooled. Explain the purpose of this control.
questions.answer: Boiled seeds are dead and do not respire, so any movement of the fluid is due to changes in temperature or air pressure and can be allowed for.
steps: Boiled seeds are dead / do not respire, so they take up no oxygen
Any movement of the fluid is due to changes in temperature or air pressure, so the results can be corrected / only respiration is measured
accept: Shows that the movement in the experiment is caused by the living seeds
Acts as a control for changes in atmospheric pressure or temperature
Boiling denatures the enzymes of respiration

questions.question: A student used a respirometer to measure the rate of oxygen uptake of 2.0 g of germinating pea seeds. The seeds were in a sealed tube that also contained a small container of potassium hydroxide solution, which absorbs carbon dioxide. The tube was connected to a horizontal capillary tube of internal diameter 1.0 mm containing a drop of coloured fluid. The fluid moved 36 mm towards the seeds in 12 minutes at a constant temperature. The respiratory quotient (RQ) is the volume of carbon dioxide produced divided by the volume of oxygen taken up. The 2.0 g of seeds took up oxygen at 2.36 mm3 min^-1 and the RQ of the seeds was 0.85. Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide produced by the seeds each minute.
questions.answer: 2.0 mm3 min^-1
steps: RQ = volume of CO2 produced / volume of O2 taken up, so CO2 produced = RQ x O2 taken up.
CO2 produced = 0.85 x 2.36 = 2.0 mm3 min^-1 (2 s.f.).

questions.question: A student used a respirometer to measure the rate of oxygen uptake of 2.0 g of germinating pea seeds. The seeds were in a sealed tube that also contained a small container of potassium hydroxide solution, which absorbs carbon dioxide. The tube was connected to a horizontal capillary tube of internal diameter 1.0 mm containing a drop of coloured fluid. The fluid moved 36 mm towards the seeds in 12 minutes at a constant temperature. The RQ is about 1.0 when carbohydrate is the respiratory substrate and about 0.7 when lipid is the respiratory substrate. Suggest what an RQ of 0.85 shows about the respiratory substrate of the germinating seeds.
questions.answer: The seeds are respiring a mixture of carbohydrate and lipid.
steps: RQ of 0.85 lies between 0.7 (lipid) and 1.0 (carbohydrate)
So a mixture of carbohydrate and lipid is being respired
accept: Protein (RQ about 0.8 to 0.9) could also be respired
A mixture of lipid, carbohydrate and protein
Pea seeds store starch and protein as well as some lipid
